Title: Passage 2: [Excerpt from] The Farm She Was: A Novel
Author: by Ann Mohin
Content: This farmhouse was built in `1845` in the center of `text(eighty-five)`, `text(half-wooded)` rolling `text(acres)`. It was a small and self-contained farm, but now its fields and pastures are fallow and overgrown. Damaged remnants of fieldstone fences limp through the trees - maple and cherry, oak and poplar, hemlock, beech, and the wild apples.

Rugged Germans `text(first)` cleared this land, leveling the dense forest with `text(two-man)` saws, pulling and burning the stumps with horses, plowing up fieldstones. With hands for machines and back-breaking labor, they used those rocks to build `text(four-foot)` high, geometrically-perfect fences. As proficient as trained masons, they selected `text(each fieldstone)` like a poet selects her words. They laid the flat stones one atop the other for `text(miles)` and `text(miles)` through the woods until the cows and the sheep could, finally, be allowed to roam. . . .

The man who built our house and cleared our fields and built the stone walls, certainly drove himself hard. Having completed his mission here in New York, he gathered his family and abandoned the state in `1859`. My father's eyes sometimes glistened when he told the story of this German immigrant whose land and home we had acquired, how he packed up his belongings and moved to Ohio. There he cleared another piece of land, built another post-and-beam house, more stone walls.

I've always wondered why he left New York to start all over again. He had built a beautiful home, and the barns and the pastures and orchards were clear of rocks. Did he leave because of the hard weather? Or was it the acidic soil of this region where field crops are limited to cabbage and corn? Could it have been that he was simply bored?

The German had an engineer's mind. The house is sited precisely to benefit from the most `text(southern sun)` and the high ridge to the `text(north)` side protects against the killer winds. My father's building skills were comparatively limited, but his carpentry was adequate and the barns and wagons were not in disrepair. Father understood the meaning of maintenance, and to keep the farm in forward motion he adequately taught himself the art of reconstruction.

When Mother complained that the house was too dark, he put windows where there were none. The forest is visible from `text(every room)` and now in `text(May)`, when finally, finally, spring can be trusted to stay, new leaves accessorize my father's handiwork like lime-colored curtains and white tufts of the early flowers sway from tender shadbush branches. I stare out this window next to my bed and yes, I do remember other seasons, other times. The seasons are still intact; to hope for more than that is a foolish exertion.
